AI-music detection · cross-domain evaluation

Who gets called AI?

6 detectors built from a pool of 12,265 ten-second clips (5,553 human, 6,712 AI from 23 generator versions; no detector trains on more than 8,494 of them), then tested where detectors usually fail: on music from sources they never saw. The question is how often a real musician gets accused.

The headline

14.0%of unseen human tracks (FMA, before 2010) falsely called AI by 3. ResNet18 on log-mel (the main detector), the lowest rate among the detectors trained here; on unseen Jamendo tracks it falsely calls 27.8% AI (the off-the-shelf SONICS SpecTTTra-α 5s, not retrained, wrongly flags only 7.6% of those FMA tracks and 6.0% of the Jamendo tracks, but it catches only 29% of matched AI tracks)
61.7%of those same FMA tracks falsely called AI by Ablation: features + LR, no file-format features
89.8%the best lab score (matched split) among detectors with all four conditions finished, from 2. Interpretable features + boosted trees. Beside it: unseen FMA tracks falsely called AI 59.6%, unseen Jamendo 34.9%; unseen generators: balanced accuracy 81.1% with one version held out (caught 70% on average, worst 1%, stable_audio_open), 70.2% with a whole family held out (11% of udio caught); balanced accuracy vocal→instrumental 64.0%, instrumental→vocal 76.4%

The model that wins in the lab is not the one that accuses the fewest unfamiliar human tracks. That is the pattern of MuseBench, where a fully trained ResNet18 scored 100% in-domain and passed only 28.4% of old FMA tracks, reproduced here on different data with different generators.

The main detector was retrained to remove a shortcut. In this data, 1,278 of the 1,295 clips whose original file was 32 kHz or lower are AI. The first ResNet18 saw frequencies up to 16 kHz and learned that missing high frequencies mean AI. It was retrained with its spectrogram capped at 7 kHz, below the lowest bandwidth of any file in the data, and no longer has that shortcut. Every number below comes from the same rounds and test clips. Genuinely old recordings are still harder than modern ones: of the 799 pre-2010 FMA tracks, the 123 with almost no sound above 8 kHz (old or lo-fi recordings, 36 of them 78-rpm transfers) are wrongly called AI 24.4% of the time, against 12.1% for the rest. Band-limiting a modern recording at 8 kHz, above the 7 kHz the detector sees, no longer changes the verdict, so the missing top octave is not the cause; whether a narrower bandwidth (most of these tracks also have little sound at 5-8 kHz) or another trait such as surface noise is the cause was not tested.

The unseen-generator columns count single-version hold-outs only. Holding out a whole family is harder (the 'ALL ...' columns in the unseen-generator figure): there the main detector, 3. ResNet18 on log-mel, averages 75.7% balanced accuracy (against 79.2%) and catches only 42% of udio tracks with every udio version held out. For the two off-the-shelf detectors, Suno v3.5 and Udio v1 are left out of these columns because those detectors were trained on them.

Unseen generators

Each AI model with at least 60 clips is removed from training in turn and the detector must still catch it. Every family with more than one version (audiocraft, lyria, mureka, riffusion, suno, udio) is also held out as a whole, because siblings share decoders and make single-version hold-outs look easier than they are. mureka_other, suno_other (too few clips) are held out only with their family.

Unseen human music

Trained with human music from one platform only, tested on another. FMA uploads from before 2010 predate AI song generators by more than a decade, so every one of them is human. GuitarSet is solo acoustic guitar, a deliberately hard case.

Vocal and instrumental

Trained on one, tested on the other, in both directions. Caveat: 65% of instrumental AI clips come from open-weight models (MusicGen, MAGNeT, Stable Audio Open, AudioLDM2...) while 65% of vocal ones come from commercial services (Suno, Udio, Mureka...), so this condition partly measures a change of generator too.

The original hypothesis: does a detector fail on a genre it never saw?

For each genre with enough test clips, the same detector is trained with and without that genre and tested on it. A large drop would support "detectors only work per genre". Genres come from a zero-shot CLAP tagger. It agrees with FMA's own genre labels on 47.2% of 2,364 FMA clips across 9 coarse genres (agreement expected by chance, given how often each genre occurs, is about 17%; always answering rock/metal would score 27%), so genre groups are noisy: treat this as a coarse test of the hypothesis. Both training sets in a pair are the same size, and a dataset that is almost all one genre (GuitarSet, solo acoustic guitar, for country/folk) is not scored in that genre's rounds: removing the genre would remove the whole dataset, which is the unseen-human question, not the genre question.

Result: removing a genre from training lowers each detector's AUC on that genre by +0.005 to +0.021 on average (AUC runs from 0.5, guessing, to 1, perfect). The largest single drop is +0.035 (4. CLAP embedding + linear head, rock_metal). Drops this small do not support "detectors only work per genre", at least for genres this coarse. The drops are small but consistent: 53 of 63 detector-genre pairs drop, and both settings score the same 85-599 test clips per genre. At the 0.5 threshold the picture is mixed: holding a genre out raises the share of human clips accused in that genre in 31 of 63 pairs, lowers it in 19 and leaves it unchanged in 13 (mean +1.1 points per pair). The largest rise is +13.6 points (4. CLAP embedding + linear head, pop: 19.0% of human clips flagged with the genre in training, 32.7% with it held out). The rise is consistent only for 4. CLAP embedding + linear head (6 of 7 genres) and 2. Interpretable features + boosted trees (6 of 7 genres), so some detectors, not all, become more suspicious of a genre they never saw. Only 7 of the 10 tagged genres have at least 30 AI and 30 human test clips and are scored. ResNet18 was not run on this condition (14 extra trainings were too slow on CPU).

Reverse engineering, done the legitimate way

Suno and Udio do not publish their architectures. What their outputs show is the decoder's upsampling grid: narrow spectral peaks at every multiple of the decoder's internal frame rate (Afchar et al., ISMIR 2025). Averaging up to 80 clips per generator (generators with fewer than 20 clips are not scanned) and testing every spacing from 12 to 400 Hz in 0.05 Hz steps shows which grids are present. Lossy file formats leave grids of their own (MP3 cuts the spectrum into 32 equal bands), so the same human clips were re-encoded in the lossy formats the AI files came in (MP3 at 48 and 44.1 kHz, AAC, Opus) and scanned the same way, and each generator's clips were split in two halves that must agree.

Check on open models first: 3 of the 3 EnCodec-32k models (MusicGen, MAGNeT, JASCO), whose published decoder predicts grids at multiples of 50 Hz, show a comb on a multiple of 50 Hz (musicgen, magnet, jasco). Stable Audio Open, whose Oobleck decoder predicts a 21.5 Hz grid, does not (contrast 0.02 dB at 21.5 Hz); its strongest grid is 349.2 Hz, which no published decoder explains. So a missing comb does not prove a model has no transposed-convolution decoder, and an unexplained one is not attributable.

  • 200 Hz grid: suno_v3.5, suno_v4, suno_v4.5, suno_v5.5, yue
  • 250 Hz grid: acestep_1.5
  • 293.6 Hz grid: riffusion_v1
  • 349.2 Hz grid: stable_audio_open
  • 400 Hz grid: jasco, magnet, musicgen

Marginal, too close to the ceiling to call: mureka_other, mustango, udio_v1.

Caution: riffusion_v1, stable_audio_open peak at a spacing where the scan's noise also peaks in human and codec-control sets (around 262, 278, 294, 330, 351, 370, 392 Hz). The comb is strong, but its exact spacing is less trustworthy than its strength.

No comb that clears both tests: audioldm2, diffrhythm, lyria_pro3, lyria_realtime, mureka_V6, riffusion_fuzz1.1, sonauto_v2, udio_v1.5. A missing grid does not make a Fourier-based detector blind: the retrained Deezer fakeprint reads the whole 5-16 kHz spectrum, not only grids. With these generators in training it caught 46%-98% of their test clips; with one of them held out, 6%-77%; and it caught only 1% of held-out riffusion_v1, which has a clear comb. So the scan is a rough guide, not a rule: held out, the fakeprint caught a median 94% of the 11 generators with a clear comb but 30% of the 8 without one, with exceptions both ways.

suno_v3.5, suno_v4, suno_v5.5, suno_v4.5 share one grid at 200 Hz, as does the open-source YuE (its X-Codec tokenizer runs at 50 frames per second). Human music re-encoded as the same 48 kHz MP3 stays below the ceiling at 200 Hz (see the table), so the grid comes from the generator, not the file format. That is consistent with a 50 Hz codec-token design across Suno's versions; it is evidence about the decoder, not proof of Suno's architecture.

Ceiling: averaged over 80 clips per set, no human set (FMA, Jamendo, GuitarSet) and no set of the same human clips re-encoded in these formats reaches more than 0.71 dB at any spacing from 12 to 400 Hz. This ceiling applies only to averages of many clips: single human recordings usually score well above it, so it must never be used to judge one song. 'Comb found' = the generator's average is above that ceiling and has the same spacing (within 1%) in two independent halves of its clips; 'marginal' = less than 0.15 dB above the ceiling, too close to call. 'Delivered as' is each generator's most common file format.

Chords and keys

The brief suggested AI tracks use non-diatonic chords and abrupt key changes. That idea comes from a qualitative look at 30 AI rock tracks in MuseBench's appendix. Corpus studies do not support it for chords: Suno and Udio score about the same as human music on a diatonic-strength measure (Cros Vila et al., TISMIR 2025, doi:10.5334/tismir.254), and a large chord-analysis study found similar chord types in all three, with Suno (up to v3.5) leaning on stock pop progressions such as I-V-vi-IV and Udio statistically close to human music (Dalmazzo et al., TISMIR 2026, doi:10.5334/tismir.348). Neither study measured key changes. The optional harmony features test both on a sample.

On 2,400 clips (100 per dataset), the non-diatonic-chord rate separates AI from human with AUC 0.45 (0.5 = no information; below 0.5 means AI tracks use fewer out-of-key chords). Key changes lean very slightly the brief's way: the share of 2.5-second windows whose key differs from the excerpt's key gives AUC 0.53, from only four windows per 10-second clip. Neither feature is a usable AI tell.

"Physical impossibility" checks (more than ten simultaneous piano notes, guitar notes outside E2-E6) were not implemented: they need reliable transcription and instrument identification inside full mixes, which no CPU-friendly open model provides, and no published detector uses them.

Data and provenance

Every clip is cut and decoded the same way (ffmpeg, soxr to 48 kHz, 16-bit, one 10-second excerpt per track). Splits never share an artist, a caption source, a held-out generator or a held-out human platform; the program stops if one does. No present-day commercial releases were downloaded: the human clips are Creative Commons or academic (FMA, Jamendo, GuitarSet). Two exceptions need a lawyer's view before publishing: 133 FMA clips (genre 'Old-Time / Historic') are digitised early-20th-century commercial 78-rpm records that FMA tags 'Sound Recording Common Law Protection', and 1,845 AI clips (Suno, Udio, Mureka, Riffusion, Sonauto) come from a scraped collection with no clear licence. No audio is redistributed.

What the brief got right, and what it got wrong

  • MuseBench is real (arXiv 2610.20310, October 2026) and its numbers check out, including the 28.4% figure.
  • Deezer's detector beats every neural model in MuseBench on unseen human music (94.4% vs at most 79.8%). In-domain it trails the five spectrogram and transformer models (97.6% vs 99.5-100%) but beats the two raw-waveform models (M5 94.3%, RawNet2 82.3%). MuseBench warns that its 94.4% may partly reflect a boundary that leans towards "human", since it misses many AI tracks from held-out generators.
  • The 5-8 kHz / 12-18 kHz bands come from one model's Grad-CAM, not from detectors in general.
  • The Velvet Sundown's bio called it "an ongoing artistic provocation"; the "spokesperson" was an impostor and the Suno claim is unconfirmed.
  • Breaking Rust's generator is unknown. No reporting says it was not Suno or Udio, so it cannot be called a confirmed unseen generator.
  • Non-diatonic chords as an AI tell is not supported by corpus studies of Suno and Udio (Cros Vila et al., TISMIR 2025; Dalmazzo et al., TISMIR 2026) or by this project's probe (AI uses fewer out-of-key chords); the only evidence for it is qualitative (MuseBench, 30 tracks). Key changes are untested in the literature and at most weakly present here. A "second-order FFT" detector is not in the literature: MuseBench uses it only as an analysis tool, and the peaks are visible in the ordinary spectrum.

Limits

  • Ten-second excerpts, CPU-only training. ResNet18 trained on at most 3,000 clips per round for 4 epochs, far less than published baselines. A longer run was not tested and could score better or worse on unseen music, including the false-positive rate on human tracks.
  • The datasets differ in sample rate, channels and bitrate. Every clip is re-decoded identically, but traces of the original format remain (see the leakage report). The main detector's spectrogram is capped below the lowest bandwidth in the data so the missing top octave of 16 and 32 kHz files cannot be used; the interpretable feature models still see the format traces, which is what the 'no file-format features' ablation and the codec-equalised variants measure.
  • Vocal labels mix metadata with an AudioSet tagger: 67% of clips were labelled by the tagger, which agrees with the known labels 78.2% of the time (balanced), so some clips sit on the wrong side of the vocal/instrumental line. Genre labels are coarse.
  • No Suno v6 or Udio v1.5 Allegro data, and no tracks generated by this project (tier A). Suno's flagship v6 models need a paid plan, and Udio has disabled audio downloads on every plan since late October 2025, so new Udio audio cannot currently be collected at all.

A detector score is evidence, not proof. Before publishing the paper, the trained models or derived data, publishing verdicts about named artists, or deploying a public tool, get legal advice: Deezer's method is patent-pending and licensed non-commercially; most datasets are non-commercial or research-only; 1,845 AI clips were scraped with no clear licence; 133 FMA clips are historic commercial records; the ResNet18 starts from ImageNet-pretrained weights; and calling a real musician "AI" can harm their career.
